parts.partTitle: JWT Anatomy and Critical Security Traps

beats.headline: Is your JWT implementation actually secure?
beats.subline: Signed does not mean encrypted. Base64 is just encoding.
beats.narration: Stateless JWTs are the standard for modern APIs, but they are riddled with pitfalls. Signed does not mean encrypted, and a single misconfiguration can let an attacker bypass your entire auth layer.

beats.title: The JWT Structure

nodes.label: Payload
nodes.detail: Claims like sub, aud, and roles

beats.narration: A JWT is just three Base64 encoded segments. The header defines the algorithm, the payload holds your user claims, and the signature ensures that no one tampered with the data.

beats.title: Signed vs. Encrypted
beats.narration: Never store PII or secrets in a standard JWT. Anyone can decode it in milliseconds. If you need confidentiality, use JWE, otherwise keep your payloads lean and public-friendly.

beats.title: Pinning the Algorithm

steps.explanation: Forces the decoder to use RSA. Rejects HS256 or none.

beats.narration: The biggest vulnerability is algorithm confusion. Never let the token header choose the algorithm. Pin it server-side to RS256 so attackers cannot force your verifier to use HMAC with a public key.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Wiring the Spring Security Filter chain →
beats.narration: That is the foundation. In Part 2, we build a custom OncePerRequestFilter to handle token extraction without double-execution bugs.

beats.headline: Is your filter running twice per request?
beats.subline: Spring Boot filter beans often trigger double-execution.
beats.narration: If you annotate your AuthFilter as a Component, Spring Boot registers it globally. It will run on every request, even public ones, destroying your performance and causing weird bugs.

beats.title: The OncePerRequestFilter

steps.explanation: Guarantees execution only once per request lifecycle.
Bypass logic for public endpoints or missing headers.

beats.narration: Extend OncePerRequestFilter to ensure your logic runs exactly once. Check the Authorization header early and return if it is missing, keeping your filter chain clean and efficient.

beats.title: Manual Registration

steps.explanation: Instantiate manually to prevent global registration.
Insert into the chain at the right priority.

beats.narration: Do not use @Component. Instantiate the filter inside your SecurityFilterChain configuration and add it before the standard username-password filter. This prevents double-execution and keeps your security logic isolated.

beats.title: Verifying the Chain

lines.text: # Check logs for filter execution count

beats.narration: Test your filter with a simple curl command. Monitor your application logs to ensure the filter logic triggers only once per request. If you see double logs, your filter is registered as a global bean.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
beats.narration: That is the filter chain handled. In Part 3, we implement Refresh Token Rotation to detect stolen tokens and limit the blast radius of a breach.

beats.headline: What happens if a token is stolen?
beats.subline: Refresh token rotation turns theft into a detectable event.
beats.narration: If a long-lived refresh token is stolen, the attacker has permanent access. Rotation forces a new token every time, and reuse detection allows you to revoke the entire session family.

beats.title: Rotation Flow
beats.narration: When the client refreshes, the server marks the old token as used and issues a new one. If the old token appears again, the server knows it was stolen and revokes the whole family.

beats.title: Detecting Reuse

steps.explanation: Check if the token has already been exchanged.
Invalidate all tokens in this session family.

beats.narration: This is the core of reuse detection. If a token is already marked as used, you have a security incident. Revoke every token associated with that family ID to stop the attacker immediately.

beats.title: Storage Strategies
beats.narration: Never store tokens in localStorage. Use HttpOnly cookies to hide them from malicious scripts. This is the single most effective way to prevent token theft in browser-based applications.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 4): Production Pitfalls & Interview Prep →
beats.narration: Rotation is your best defense against token theft. In Part 4, we wrap up with production pitfalls and the interview questions that separate seniors from juniors.

beats.headline: Why do microservices fail at JWT auth?
beats.subline: The secret is in the audience claim and key management.
beats.narration: Most teams fail by using symmetric keys or ignoring the audience claim. These are the exact questions interviewers use to test your understanding of distributed security.

beats.title: Symmetric vs. Asymmetric
beats.narration: Always prefer asymmetric signing. If a downstream service is compromised, the attacker cannot mint new tokens because they only have the public key. Shared secrets are a liability.

beats.title: The Audience Claim

lines.text: Prevents token replay across different APIs!

beats.narration: The audience claim is non-negotiable. It ensures a token issued for a catalog service cannot be replayed against a billing service. Always validate the aud claim in your decoder.

beats.title: Revocation via JTI

steps.explanation: Unique token ID for replay prevention.
Check this cache before trusting any token.

beats.narration: Need to revoke a token before it expires? Store the JTI in Redis with a TTL. Check the cache during validation. It keeps your stateless architecture performant while adding immediate revocation.

beats.title: Chapter Complete
beats.narration: You have mastered stateless auth. Checkout the branch to run the full lab and verify your security configuration. See you in the next chapter.
